lesson.title: Spans and subspaces

lead.text: Start with the one-button remote. Each press moves the robot by the vector (1, 2), which is one tile across and two up. Two presses take it to (2, 4), three to (3, 6), and one press of the backwards button takes it to (−1, −2). Every place it can reach is the move multiplied by some number c, so every reachable place has the form c(1, 2).

Plot those places and they fall on one straight line that runs through the starting tile in both directions. A tile off that line, such as (1, 3), can never be reached with this remote. The set of everything the robot can reach has a name: it is the span of the vector (1, 2). More generally, the span of some vectors is every vector you can build from them by scaling and adding.

afterFigure.text: With one button the span is a line, and the figure shows two examples. A line gives the robot a single direction to travel in, which it can follow either way. To leave the line the robot needs a second button, which is where we go next.

lead.text: The remote has only the (1, 2) button and its backwards twin. The robot has stopped at a place whose across coordinate is 3.

reveal.text: Three presses reach (3, 6). Every reachable place is a multiple of (1, 2), so the up coordinate is always double the across coordinate.

lead.text: Now give the remote a second button that moves the robot by (1, 0), one tile across and none up. The robot can press both buttons in any mix. Press the first button twice and the second three times, and it ends at 2(1, 2) + 3(1, 0) = (2, 4) + (3, 0) = (5, 4). A total of that kind, with each move scaled by a number and the results added, is a combination of the two moves.

The span of the two moves is the set of all their combinations, and here it is the whole floor. The up coordinate of any combination comes only from the first button, so it settles how many presses that button needs. The second button then makes up whatever is missing across. Every tile can be reached this way.

afterFigure.text: Not every second button helps. Give the robot (2, 4) as its second move and it already had that: two presses of the first button make it. The new button adds no new direction, and the span stays the same line. The number of independent directions in a span is its dimension, so a line has dimension 1 and the whole floor has dimension 2. Two moves reach dimension 2 only when neither is a scaled copy of the other, and a scaled copy can point backwards, as (−1, −2) does.

lead.text: The remote has the buttons (1, 2) and (2, 4), each with a backwards twin.

reveal.text: You checked whether the second button adds a direction. A scaled copy gives nothing new, so the span stays a line.

lead.text: Now run the question backwards. The remote has the buttons (1, 0) and (1, 1), and the robot stands at (4, 1). How many presses of each button put it there? Call the two numbers c₁ and c₂, so that (4, 1) = c₁(1, 0) + c₂(1, 1). These numbers are the coefficients of the combination.

One vector equation hides one ordinary equation for each coordinate, and one of the two is easy. Look at the up coordinates. The button (1, 0) has no up part, so all of the up distance, 1, must come from the second button, and c₂ = 1. The across coordinates then say c₁ + c₂ = 4, and since c₂ is now known, c₁ = 3.

Check it by pressing: 3(1, 0) + 1(1, 1) = (3, 0) + (1, 1) = (4, 1). The habit to take away is to match one coordinate at a time, starting with the coordinate where only one button contributes. If no coefficients work, the target lies outside the span.

steps.headline: A set that stays inside itself

lead.text: Every span we have met has one property worth noticing. Take the line through (1, 2) and pick two places on it, (2, 4) and (−1, −2). Their sum is (1, 2), which is on the line again. Scale (2, 4) by 5 and you get (10, 20), which is also on the line. Whichever way you add places on the line or scale them, the robot never leaves it.

A set of vectors with that behaviour is called a subspace. It has to contain the zero vector, and it has to stay inside itself, so that adding two members or scaling one always gives another member. The zero vector belongs because scaling any member by 0 produces it: a robot that presses nothing stays on its starting tile.

afterFigure.text: Every span is a subspace, because a sum of combinations of the same moves is another combination of them, and so is a scaled one. The line and the whole floor are both examples. The zero vector also gives a quick way to rule a set out: if a set misses it, the set cannot be a subspace.

steps.headline: A line that misses the start

lead.text: A straight line is not always a subspace. Take the points (x, y) with y = x + 3, a line that runs parallel to the diagonal through the starting tile but sits three units higher. The zero vector would need 0 = 0 + 3, which fails, so the starting tile is not on this line and the first requirement is broken.

The second requirement breaks too. The points (0, 3) and (1, 4) are both on the line, since 3 = 0 + 3 and 4 = 1 + 3. Their sum is (1, 7), and 7 is not 1 + 3 = 4, so adding two members has left the set.
The test has two parts. First ask whether the zero vector is in the set. If it is, ask whether adding and scaling keep you inside. The first question often settles the matter alone, as it does here.
Consider the line made of all points whose up distance is double their across distance.

reveal.text: That line is the span of (1, 2), so it contains the zero vector and stays inside itself under adding and scaling.

lead.text: A delivery drone is allowed to fly only along one straight path, and its pilot wants to treat the path as a space of its own.

lesson.orientation: Describe all linear combinations and test the conditions for a subspace.

blocks.text: The last lesson ended with solutions that fill out a line or a plane, whatever the number of unknowns. Those shapes turn up all through linear algebra, and a toy robot is a good way to meet them.

Picture the robot on a huge floor of square tiles, with you holding its remote. The remote has a single button. Each press moves the robot one tile across and two tiles up, and a second button runs the same move backwards. You mark the tile it starts on, and you can press as often as you like.

Some tiles are within reach and most are not. This lesson looks at the whole set of reachable tiles, at how it grows as the remote gets more buttons, and at which collections of tiles are tidy enough to count as a space of their own.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the dimension of a span and test whether a set is a subspace.

recap.keyIdea: A span is every combination of some vectors, and its dimension counts the independent directions. A subspace contains zero and stays inside itself under adding and scaling.

blocks.text: Back at the robot's remote, you saw that one button keeps it on a line and a second, different button frees it across the floor. You wrote (4, 1), (7, 4) and (5, 3) as combinations of two moves, and you ruled out a path that misses the starting tile.

recap.nextHook: Some remotes carry a button the robot never needed, such as (2, 4) beside (1, 2). The next lesson asks how few buttons still reach everywhere, and what that number says about the space.
